title: Make me an instrument
hook: the prayer called Francis's comes from long after him, but carries his spirit

segments.voice: Yesterday, brother and sister creatures: sun, water, wolf, even death, all family. Your line was family of creation. Which creature did you thank out loud? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.

There's a prayer that turns up on cards, on kitchen walls, on the backs of service sheets, and it is sometimes printed with a name underneath: Saint Francis. It begins by asking to be made an instrument of peace. Here's the surprise. It isn't in anything we have from Francis's own time. Those who've traced it find it long after him, in French, in a small church publication, with no author's name at all. Somewhere along the way it picked up his name and kept it. So why does it carry his name so easily? Some readers say it's because it sounds like him. Today: make me an instrument.
screen: `A PRAYER WITH HIS NAME ON IT.`

segments.voice: The prayer is built in two halves. The first is a list of swaps. Where there's hatred, it asks to bring love. Where there's injury, pardon. Then doubt and faith, despair and hope, darkness and light, sadness and joy. Each line asks to carry into a room the opposite of what's already in it. The second half turns the usual wish around. It asks not so much to be consoled as to console, to be understood as to understand, to be loved as to love. And it ends with reversals that sound like the Gospel: it is in giving that we receive, in pardoning that we are pardoned, in dying that we are born to eternal life. Now the word instrument. Paul uses it in his letter to the Romans: "yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God." An instrument doesn't play itself. A violin doesn't pick the tune. It only has to be in tune, and in the right hands. That's the humility in this prayer. It doesn't promise to make peace by sheer effort. It asks to be used. And Jesus blessed exactly that work: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." So does it matter that Francis didn't write it? Set it beside what we've heard this week: the clothes handed back, the cold gate borne patiently, the wolf called brother. It was written far from Assisi, long after him, and some readers still hear his voice in it. A prayer can carry a saint's spirit without carrying his signature.

Here's the practice: pray it once. If you know the prayer, or have it nearby, and you pray, say it once, slowly, letting each pair land before the next. If you pray but don't know it, you can take Jesus's line instead: blessed are the peacemakers. If you don't pray, choose one pair from the list, hatred and love, despair and hope, and sit with one place in your life where that swap is needed. Breathe. The bell holds the time.
Make me an instrument. The opening request of the peace prayer that carries Francis's name: not to do great things, but to be used for peace.
Your line: an instrument of peace. Today, walk into one tense room, a group chat, a kitchen, a meeting, and bring in the opposite of what's there. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Christians in a range of churches pray the Peace Prayer, known as the Prayer of Saint Francis, alone or together, and it is also sung as a hymn.

match.prompt: the peace prayer — tap the pairs.

myth: Francis wrote the peace prayer himself
it isn't in anything from his own time; it turns up long after him, in French, unsigned.
Paul writes of yielding your members as instruments of righteousness
in his letter to the Romans: instruments of righteousness unto God.
the prayer's second half asks above all to be understood and loved
it turns that around: to understand rather than be understood, to love rather than be loved.

fork.setup: a friend shows you a card: the Prayer of Saint Francis. who wrote it?
options: Francis himself, in his own lifetime.
an unnamed writer, in French, long after him.
Brother Leo, writing down what Francis said.
fork.reveal: it appears long after Francis, in French, with no author's name. it carries his spirit, not his signature.

original.note: Greek in Romans 6:13 for instruments: tools, or weapons, put to a purpose.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old prayer written by Saint Francis.
what it means: a prayer asking to be used for peace, in his spirit though not by his hand.
what a scholar hears: it surfaces in French long after Francis, unsigned; Paul's word for instruments, hopla, can also mean weapons.

sources.ref: The Peace Prayer ('Prayer of Saint Francis'), anonymous, first printed in French

notes: Claims rule: the index hook says the prayer is 'from around 1912'. The script and hook field avoid the year and say 'centuries later, in French, in a small church publication, with no author's name' (it is usually traced to La Clochette, 1912). Confirm, and restore the year if a Keeper can cite it.
The prayer is described, not quoted, since English versions may be under copyright. The pairs and closing reversals are summarized; confirm the summary.
Practice 'pray it once' follows the outline; it invites someone who knows the prayer to say it, and offers Matthew 5:9 otherwise. No new prayer is written.
howItsDone: 'a range of churches' is a general description; confirm.
Original: ὅπλα in Romans 6:13 (ὅπλα ἀδικίας / ὅπλα δικαιοσύνης); also means weapons. Confirm.
'turns up on cards, on kitchen walls, on the backs of service sheets' is a general description; confirm.

Editor pass: 'centuries later' (an uncited time span) became 'long after him' in hook, myth and fork; 'because it sounds like him' and the claim that the unknown writer heard Francis's voice are now given as what some readers say.
